name: Los Poblanos Farm Shop
who: Farm shop on a historic lavender farm and inn, set in restored 1930s dairy barns, selling lavender goods, Farm Foods pantry items and baked goods.
why: A working farm's retail core built into real historic architecture, drawing people who plan trips around it.
takeaway: Go for lavender goods and pantry staples inside restored 1930s dairy barns on a historic lavender farm.

name: Polyface Farm Store
who: On-farm store at Joel Salatin's regenerative farm, selling pastured meat, eggs and dairy direct from the pastures.
why: The farm store that put regenerative grazing and direct-farm retail on the map, made famous by The Omnivore's Dilemma and Food, Inc.
takeaway: Go for pastured meat, eggs and dairy straight off the pastures Salatin made famous in The Omnivore's Dilemma.

name: White Oak Pastures General Store
who: General store on a sixth-generation regenerative cattle ranch, selling the farm's own grass-fed beef, poultry and tallow soap on-site.
why: A pilgrimage site for the regenerative-agriculture movement, built around a documented zero-waste, whole-animal model.
takeaway: A regenerative-ranch general store — go for the farm's own grass-fed beef, poultry and tallow soap, made on-site.

name: Shelburne Farms Farm Store & Welcome Center
who: Farm store on a historic 1,400-acre Lake Champlain estate turned nonprofit, selling farmhouse cheddar and maple syrup made on-site.
why: One of the oldest working-farm retail experiences in the US, pairing legacy architecture with hands-on food production.
takeaway: Go for the farmhouse cheddar and maple syrup made right on this historic Lake Champlain estate.

name: FARMshop
who: Bakery-and-market inside the 1948 Brentwood Country Mart, stocking curated organic produce, cheeses, chocolate and wine alongside its restaurant.
why: A market built directly into an LA architectural landmark, functioning as both grocer and neighborhood ritual.
takeaway: Go for curated cheeses, chocolate and wine inside a 1948 LA architectural landmark that doubles as a neighborhood ritual.

name: Mr Vitamins
who: Independent Australian vitamin and supplement retailer since the 1970s, stocking supplements, sports nutrition and healthy foods.
why: A rare independent supplement retailer that outlasted chain competitors by building deep category expertise.
takeaway: Go for genuine supplement expertise — a rare independent that outlasted the chains on category knowledge alone.

name: ZERO Market
who: Colorado's package-free grocery pioneer inside the Stanley Marketplace, stocking over 1,200 bulk and zero-waste pantry, body-care and cleaning goods since 2017.
why: One of the earliest and longest-running zero-waste grocery stores in the US, a model newer package-free shops point back to.
takeaway: Go for 1,200-plus package-free pantry, body-care and cleaning goods — one of the US's earliest zero-waste grocers.

name: Nude Foods Market
who: Package-free grocery with Boulder and Denver storefronts, selling bulk pantry staples, produce and prepared meals in returnable glass jars.
why: Proves the package-free grocery model can work outside the biggest cities, with a returnable-jar system as its signature.
takeaway: Go for the returnable-glass-jar system proving package-free grocery works outside the biggest cities too.

name: The Alchemist's Kitchen
who: SoHo apothecary and elixir bar selling herbal tinctures, medicinal mushrooms, CBD and wellness tonics, with in-house herbalist consultations.
why: Helped define the modern plant-medicine retail concept that later spread across US wellness culture.
takeaway: Go for tinctures, medicinal mushrooms and an in-house herbalist consult at the shop that defined plant-medicine retail.

name: Anima Mundi Apothecary
who: Herbal apothecary and tonic bar founded in Brooklyn, now with SoHo and Los Angeles locations, known for adaptogenic elixirs and vivid packaging.
why: One of the most photographed herbal apothecaries in the US, credited with mainstreaming the modern tonic-bar aesthetic.
takeaway: Go for adaptogenic elixirs in the vividly packaged apothecary that mainstreamed the whole tonic-bar aesthetic.

name: Remedies Herb Shop
who: Small-batch herbal apothecary with Brooklyn and Woodstock, NY stores, curating loose organic herbs and tinctures from about 27 independent herbal makers.
why: A community-anchored herb shop that champions small US herbalists over mass-market supplement brands.
takeaway: Go for loose organic herbs from about 27 small US herbalists, not mass-market supplement brands.

name: The Goods Mart
who: A better-for-you corner-store concept in South Williamsburg stocking healthier snacks and drinks from independent, founder-led brands.
why: Reinvents the convenience store itself as health-food retail, a genuinely new format for the segment.
takeaway: Go for the convenience store reinvented as health-food retail — snacks from independent, founder-led brands.
